analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 3, open-label, multicenter, randomized 1:1**, N=563. OS interim analysis at 243 events (**61% IF**), two-sided boundary 0.008. Data cutoff 7 Jul 2026.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: ES-SCLC after **4 cycles platinum-etoposide + durvalumab** induction with **no disease progression**, ECOG PS 0-1, age ≥18. **Asymptomatic untreated or treated brain mets allowed.**

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Tarlatamab 10 mg Q2W + durvalumab 1500 mg Q4W** vs durvalumab 1500 mg Q4W alone, 28-day cycles, until progression or toxicity. On-site monitoring 1-2h (6-8h in some regions) after early tarlatamab doses.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: OS.** Key secondary: PFS. Secondary: ORR, DOR, safety. Tested hierarchically OS → PFS → ORR.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Control arm is the current chemo-IO maintenance standard established by CASPIAN-era durvalumab, so the comparator is contemporary. Tarlatamab previously moved into later lines (DeLLphi-304); this trial tests it earlier, in the maintenance window.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ES-SCLC nonprogressors after platinum-etoposide + durvalumab, ECOG 0-1. Does not represent pts who progressed on induction, ECOG ≥2, or atezolizumab-based induction.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Efficacy stop at **61% IF** risks an inflated HR; median FU ~16 mo leaves the OS tail unknown. **No safety data in source**, and thoracic RT/PCI permissibility not stated.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A BiTE added at the point of maximal disease control nearly halves the death hazard over durvalumab alone. Unsettled: toxicity cost, durability beyond the interim, and integration with consolidative RT.

studies.interpretation:
The comparator here matters most. Durvalumab maintenance after platinum-etoposide plus durvalumab is the backbone that CASPIAN made standard, so this is not a win over an outdated control. Adding tarlatamab at the point of best disease control, rather than holding it for relapse as DeLLphi-304 did, gives an OS HR of 0.42 and a median OS of 21.1 vs 12.7 mo. In ES-SCLC, where first-line chemo-IO gains have been measured in a few months, an effect this size is unusual. The PFS HR of 0.34 points the same way, and because the hierarchy was OS → PFS → ORR, the secondary endpoints are confirmatory and were not picked after the fact.

Three features of the design should temper confidence in the exact size of the effect, though probably not in its direction. First, the OS analysis was an interim look at 243 events, 61% of the planned information, against a two-sided boundary of 0.008. Trials that stop early for efficacy tend to overestimate the true effect, so a fully mature HR could land closer to 1 than 0.42 and still be clinically decisive. Second, median follow-up of about 16 months is short next to the experimental arm's median. Its median OS has a non-estimable upper bound (20.8-NE), so whether the curves stay apart or a durable tail forms, the way IO tails formed in this disease, is not yet known. Third, the trial was open-label. OS resists that bias, but PFS and response assessment do not. Still, the PFS result fits the OS result well enough that bias is unlikely to explain it.

Generalizability is the larger question. Only patients who reached maintenance without progression and kept ECOG 0-1 were eligible. That is a selected subset of the ES-SCLC population at diagnosis, enriched for chemosensitive disease. The result says nothing about patients who progress during induction or decline in performance status. Allowing asymptomatic untreated brain metastases, with brain/liver metastases as a stratification factor, widens the population compared with many SCLC trials. But the source does not give the subgroup estimate, so it cannot show whether intracranial disease shares the benefit.

The source also leaves out what a treating physician most needs to weigh against the survival gain: rates of cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity and grade 3+ events. The protocol's required post-dose monitoring (1-2 hours, or 6-8 hours in some regions, after early doses) shows the operational cost but not the clinical one. The tweet notes that 44% of patients were still on the combination at cutoff, which suggests tolerability was not prohibitive. That is indirect evidence, not a safety profile.

For a radiation oncologist, the open issue is how this fits with consolidative thoracic RT and cranial management. The source does not say whether thoracic RT or PCI was allowed. A maintenance regimen this active changes the context in which consolidation decisions are made. It does not settle whether RT still adds to it, or how a T-cell engager combines with thoracic or cranial irradiation. This result moves the systemic maintenance decision for induction nonprogressors. The RT consolidation question remains open until data on that interaction exist.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: Adds a BiTE to durvalumab maintenance with an OS HR of 0.42 and mOS 21.1 vs 12.7 mo, moving tarlatamab from later-line into 1L maintenance for induction nonprogressors. The post-dose monitoring requirement (1-2h, 6-8h in some regions) is an operational cost to plan for; AE rates are not in the source.

studies.name: SBRT for Ultra-Central Lung Tumors Meta-Analysis
studies.tldr: Pooled 1-yr LC 92% and 2-yr LC 89% after ultra-central lung SBRT; G5 toxicity 4%, mostly hemoptysis, across 27 mostly retrospective studies.

details.text: 🔍 27 studies (2010-2022), 1183 pts; all retrospective except HILUS phase II, none randomized
🔍 UC definition varied: PTV-PBT overlap in 100% of studies, GTV overlap in only 59%
🔍 Dose 30-70 Gy in 3-10 fx; BED10 range 52.5-180
🔍 Commonest schedules: 50 Gy/5 (18%), 60 Gy/8 (17%), 60 Gy/12 (10%)
📊 Pooled outcomes (random effects)
📊 Primary NSCLC subset: 1- and 2-yr LC both 95%
📐 Meta-regression: higher BED tied to 1-yr LC (HR 2.14, p=0.03); no 2-yr association (p=0.66)

📊 73 G5 events; hemoptysis most common (42 events, 58% of G5)
⚠️ Fatal-toxicity risk factors across pooled series

verdict.rationale: Pooled retrospective series (one prospective, none randomized) with I² >90% for LC, publication bias on every endpoint, and inconsistent ultra-central definitions. Guideline layer is expert opinion.
verdict.audience: Ultra-central lung tumors (primary NSCLC or mets), PTV abutting/overlapping PBT

studies.significance: The toxicity signal follows PBT hot spots, not the prescription: HILUS's 15% G5 came with a 67% IDL and median main bronchus Dmax 97 Gy. ISRS response: prescribe to 80-85% IDL, cap PBT Dmax at 133-150 Gy BED3 (EQD23 80-90 Gy), undercover PTV before overdosing airway.
studies.monday_clinic: In an ultra-central lung tumor without endobronchial extension or ILD, this supports 60 Gy/8 or 60 Gy/15 with a strict PBT hot-spot limit; it does not extend to endobronchial disease, where ISRS favors 60 Gy/15 with PBT Dmax <100 Gy BED3.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA/MOOSE) of **27 studies, 1183 pts**, published 2010-2022; random-effects pooling with meta-regression. **All retrospective except HILUS** (prospective phase II); none randomized. Median f/u ranged 7.6-44.5 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Ultra-central lung tumors treated with SBRT (**≥5 Gy/fx**, photons), ≥5 eligible lesions per study. Excluded reirradiation and hilar/mediastinal nodal targets. Histology mixed; 9 studies (33%) were entirely primary NSCLC.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Dose 30-70 Gy in 3-10 fx, most often **50 Gy/5, 60 Gy/8, 60 Gy/12**. Motion management in 96% of studies, mostly 4DCT. OAR dosimetry reporting was variable.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **1-yr LC 92%** (95% CI 86-96), **2-yr LC 89%** (82-94); primary NSCLC subset 95% at both timepoints. Higher BED tracked with 1-yr LC (**HR 2.14, p=0.03**), not 2-yr (p=0.66).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **Any G3-4 6%** (3-10), **any G5 4%** (2-6), G5 hemoptysis 1% (0-3). G5 ≥10% in 7 studies; HILUS 15%. Risk factors: endobronchial tumor, antiplatelet/anticoagulant use, **VEGF inhibitor within 30 days (HR 16.9)**, ILD.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Pooled 2-yr LC sits beside RTOG 0813 (89.4% in central/UC tumors). A prior 250-pt systematic review reported higher toxicity (treatment-related mortality 5%, G≥3 10%); the authors attribute the lower rates here to more contemporary, conformal series.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ultra-central primary NSCLC and lung metastases with PTV overlap of the PBT, treated with BED10-oriented SBRT and motion management. Does not represent endobronchial tumors, ILD, hilar/mediastinal nodal targets, or reirradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Fig 3 dose-event mapping drew on only 37 events from 9 studies, and **PBT substructure dosimetry was rarely reported**, so constraints beyond HILUS's could not be derived. Toxicity attribution in retrospective series is open to misclassification.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Efficacy is not the question; airway dose is. The ISRS constraint (**PBT Dmax <133-150 Gy BED3**) is built from cross-series convergence of fatal-hemoptysis doses, not a modeled threshold, and is pending SUNSET and LUNGTECH.

studies.interpretation:
The efficacy half of this paper is the less contested half. A pooled 2-year local control of 89% lands where RTOG 0813 did for central and ultra-central tumors, and the BED dose-response on 1-year control echoes the long-standing BED10 ≥100 Gy principle. Heterogeneity above 90% makes the point estimate soft, but no plausible reweighting moves local control into a range that would argue against SBRT on efficacy grounds. The live question for ultra-central disease has always been whether the airway tolerates it, and that is where the paper should be read.

On toxicity, the 4% pooled G5 rate looks reassuring next to HILUS's 15%, but the two numbers are not measuring the same thing. HILUS was prospective, with mandated reporting, and it prescribed to a 67% isodose line with PTV margins up to 15 mm, so the central PTV ran near 150% and the main bronchus median Dmax reached 97 Gy. The retrospective series that drive the pooled estimate have the opposite bias: events are ascertained after the fact, attribution of a terminal hemoptysis to treatment versus progression is discretionary, and 60% of studies had median follow-up under two years in a toxicity whose timing extends past that. Publication bias was detected on every toxicity endpoint. A reader should treat 4% as a floor for ultra-central SBRT delivered in experienced centers, not as the expected rate.

The more durable contribution is the dosimetric synthesis. The meta-regression found no relationship between PBT Dmax and airway toxicity, and the authors are right that this reflects how few studies reported usable dosimetry rather than an absence of effect. The argument instead rests on convergence across individual series: fatal hemoptysis in Tekatli, Wang, Mihai and HILUS clusters at airway doses well above the 133-150 Gy BED3 constraint proposed, and the Fig 3 mapping places events disproportionately near the trachea and main bronchi. That is a reasonable basis for a conservative planning target, but it is expert inference from case-level data, not a dose-response model, and HILUS's substructure finding (4% vs 18% G5 hemoptysis by distance from the main bronchi) suggests a single PBT constraint is too coarse.

The risk-factor layer may matter more in clinic than the dose number. Endobronchial extension, antiplatelet or anticoagulant exposure, VEGF inhibitors near treatment, and ILD recur across the fatal cases. These are identifiable before simulation, and the guideline's practical move is to shift those patients toward 60 Gy/15 with tighter constraints rather than to abandon RT. The VEGF hazard ratio comes from one retrospective series and carries wide uncertainty, but the direction is consistent with the abdominopelvic SBRT experience.

What this does not settle: whether 60 Gy/8 and 60 Gy/15 differ in toxicity at matched airway dose, whether any constraint holds for tumors abutting the trachea itself, and whether adaptive MR-guided delivery changes the calculus. For the result to be wrong in the reassuring direction, the retrospective series would need to be undercounting fatal events by a factor near the gap with HILUS, which is not implausible. SUNSET and LUNGTECH are the prospective tests.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Airway hot spots drive fatal toxicity: HILUS's 15% G5 came with a 67% IDL and median main bronchus Dmax 97 Gy. ISRS asks for 80-85% IDL prescriptions, PBT Dmax <133-150 Gy BED3, and 60 Gy/15 with PBT Dmax <100 Gy BED3 for endobronchial disease.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Concurrent systemic agents are a modifiable risk: VEGF inhibitor within 30 days of SBRT carried fatal hemoptysis HR 16.9 in one 88-pt series. ISRS asks for 3-4 wk around VEGF inhibitors, 2-3 days for targeted agents, ≥2 days for IO, and holding antiplatelet/anticoagulation when safe.

sites.intro: ARPI intensification on top of local therapy is the theme: darolutamide with RT + ADT (DASL-HiCaP), apalutamide around RP (PROTEUS), abiraterone with ADT+docetaxel (PEACE-1).

studies.name: PEACE-1
studies.tldr: mOS 6.2 vs 4.4y (HR 0.68) adding abiraterone to ADT+docetaxel at 8y FU, n=710; no treatment-by-volume interaction (P=0.5552).

details.text: 📊 ADT+docetaxel population (n=710): abiraterone triplet vs doublet

details: 🔍 8y FU long-term analysis, restricted to the ADT+docetaxel population (n=710)
🔍 Results reported by metastatic extent (volume): high vs low
📐 No treatment-by-volume interaction for OS, p=0.5552
⚠️ Low-volume OS HR 0.74 (0.51-1.05), p=0.091: CI crosses 1, few events (67 vs 60)
⚠️ Low-volume rPFS gain is clear, HR 0.54 (0.32-0.91); OS separation lags it
🔍 SOC arms were ± prostate RT (RXT); Cox models adjusted for prostate RT, ECOG, castration type
⚠️ Abiraterone effect by RT arm not reported in source; RT-attributable effect not reported in source
⚠️ Slides report 7-yr OS/rPFS by volume; tweet's 8-yr OS is the pooled docetaxel population
📐 rPFS shown with 99.9% CI, OS with 95.1% CI

verdict.audience: Metastatic prostate cancer on ADT+docetaxel, high or low volume

studies.significance: Low volume is where prostate RT sits, and abiraterone still more than doubled 7-yr rPFS there (43.4% vs 20.9%, HR 0.54) with no volume interaction (p=0.5552). Models adjusted for prostate RT, but an abiraterone-by-RT interaction is not reported in source, so this does not settle whether triplet and prostate RT add independently.
studies.monday_clinic: In metastatic prostate cancer starting ADT+docetaxel, this supports abiraterone intensification in both high- and low-volume disease; it does not address pts not receiving docetaxel.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Randomized trial, **8y FU long-term analysis** presented at ESMO (Madrid). This report is restricted to the **ADT+docetaxel population (n=710)**, split by metastatic extent.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **High volume:** n=224 Abi vs n=231 SOC. **Low volume:** n=131 Abi vs n=124 SOC.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: SOC (ADT+docetaxel, **± prostate RT**) with vs without **abiraterone**. Dose and schedule not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Prostate RT was a factor within SOC ("+/- RXT"); Cox models **adjusted for prostate RT**. RT dose, fractionation and the abiraterone effect within each RT stratum are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Pooled OS benefit holds at 8y; volume-specific OS and rPFS are in the figure tables. **No treatment-by-volume interaction** (p=0.5552).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Extends the earlier PEACE-1 triplet result with longer follow-up and sits alongside ARASENS as the second ARPI + docetaxel triplet dataset. No cross-trial figures in source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with metastatic prostate cancer receiving ADT+docetaxel, high or low volume. Does not represent pts treated without docetaxel.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Low-volume OS rests on **67 vs 60 events** with CI 0.51-1.05. Post-progression therapy, abiraterone exposure and safety at 8y are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The absence of interaction argues against restricting the triplet to high-volume disease, even though low-volume OS has not cleared significance on its own. The rPFS signal in low volume is as large as in high volume, so the OS gap more likely reflects event count and the longer natural history of low-volume disease.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this update is durability. With eight years of follow-up in the docetaxel population, abiraterone keeps an OS advantage (median 6.2 vs 4.4 years, HR 0.68) and the 8-year survival gap (40.3% vs 27.1%) has not closed. Benefit from adding a second agent to docetaxel could plausibly have faded as control-arm pts received abiraterone or another ARPI at progression. It hasn't, which supports giving the agent upfront rather than holding it for later. The source does not report post-progression therapy, though, so how much crossover dilutes the estimate is unknown.

The volume analysis is what changes the practical argument. Doublet docetaxel has long been associated with high-volume disease, so a natural guess was that triplet intensification would earn its toxicity only there. These data don't support that guess. The interaction test is clearly null (p=0.5552). The low-volume rPFS hazard ratio (0.54) is essentially the same as the high-volume one (0.50), and 7-year rPFS in low volume roughly doubles (43.4% vs 20.9%). The low-volume OS hazard ratio of 0.74 with an interval reaching 1.05 is a power problem, not evidence of no effect. With only 67 and 60 deaths, and a control arm already at a 6.2-year median, the subgroup could not resolve a modest OS difference. Reading p=0.091 as "no benefit in low volume" would be the classic error of treating a subgroup's non-significance as heterogeneity, and the formal test says there is none.

For a radiation oncologist the more interesting question is the one the slides leave unanswered. PEACE-1 crossed abiraterone with prostate RT, and these Cox models adjust for RT, but the source does not show the abiraterone effect within the RT and no-RT strata. Low-volume disease is exactly where prostate RT is used. So the question of whether abiraterone and local RT act independently, or whether part of the systemic benefit in low volume overlaps with what local therapy provides, is still open. Until that breakdown is shown, the data support using both together without telling us how much each adds.

The statistics need one caveat. rPFS intervals are given at 99.9% and OS at 95.1%, consistent with a multiplicity-adjusted design, and the slides report 7-year landmarks by volume while the headline tweet gives 8-year pooled figures. Neither undermines the read, but readers should not line up the 7-year subgroup and 8-year pooled percentages as if they came from the same time point.

Set against ARASENS, the field now has two trials pointing the same way: in pts fit for docetaxel, adding an ARPI improves survival. This update does not choose between agents, and it says nothing about pts for whom docetaxel is not planned. What would make it wrong is a later finding that the low-volume OS estimate was driven by imbalance in post-progression therapy or RT use, and the source gives no way to check either.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Low volume is the prostate RT population, and abiraterone still lifted 7-yr rPFS 43.4% vs 20.9% there. Models adjusted for prostate RT, but abiraterone effect by RT stratum is not reported in source, so additivity with local RT remains untested here.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The volume-agnostic read is the decision point: no interaction (p=0.5552), and low-volume rPFS HR 0.54 matches high-volume 0.50. Low-volume OS HR 0.74 (0.51-1.05) reflects few events, not absent effect, so volume alone is a weak reason to withhold abiraterone from a docetaxel doublet.

open_questions: Is abiraterone benefit independent of concurrent prostate RT?
Will low-volume OS benefit reach significance with more events?
Abiraterone vs darolutamide as the triplet partner

studies.name: DASL-HiCaP
studies.tldr: 4-yr MFS-CI 95% vs 88%, HR 0.42, adding darolutamide to prostate/bed + pelvic LN RT and 96 wk ADT in very high-risk prostate cancer.
details: 🔍 International phase 3, randomized 1:1, placebo-controlled, N=1,106 (553 per arm)
💊 Darolutamide 600 mg BID x 96 wk vs placebo, both arms on 96 wk ADT

details.text: 🔍 Eligibility: DASL very high-risk features
subdetails: Radical RT: ISUP GG5, GG4 with cT2b-T4 / rT3a-T4 / PSA >20 ng/mL, or cN1
Salvage RT: PSA persistence or rise ≥0.1 ng/mL within 12 mo, plus pN1/cN1, GG5, or GG4 with pT3a-pT4

details: 🔍 RT field in both arms: prostate/bed + pelvic LNs; dose/fractionation not in source
🔍 Stratified by prior RP, planned docetaxel, and clinical/pathological pelvic N1
⚠️ Interim analysis at 87 of 130 planned MFS-CI events (67%); p=0.0001 crossed the 0.012 boundary
⚠️ MFS benefit is metastasis-driven; deaths without prior mets were balanced (see MFS figure)
⚠️ PCSS and OS CIs cross 1 at interim; OS immature
⚠️ MFS by conventional imaging; no AE rates in source, authors report burden similar to placebo
🔗 Same question as ENZARAD and the STAMPEDE M0 abiraterone comparison: ARPI on top of RT + ADT

figures.caption: Schema: 1,106 participants, R 1:1. Darolutamide 600 mg twice daily x 96 weeks vs placebo, both with RT + 96 weeks of ADT.

verdict.rationale: Clean placebo-controlled phase 3, but this is the interim analysis (87/130 events). MFS is a surrogate and OS is immature. The prespecified final analysis is the gate.
verdict.audience: Very high-risk or N1 prostate, radical or early salvage RT + 2y ADT

studies.significance: Every metastasis-free survival (MFS) difference comes from metastases (9 vs 46). Deaths without prior metastases were 18 vs 17. Both arms got prostate/bed plus pelvic nodal RT with 96 wk ADT, so this is darolutamide on top of an already intensified RT backbone, in both radical and salvage settings. RT dose was not reported.
studies.monday_clinic: For a very high-risk patient (GG5, GG4 with adverse T stage or PSA, or cN1/pN1) planned for pelvic nodal RT with 2y ADT, this supports discussing darolutamide intensification. It does not extend to shorter ADT courses or to RT without nodal coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International, **randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3**, 1:1, **N=1,106**. Enrolment April 2020 to August 2023. **Interim analysis** triggered at the 87th MFS-CI event (67%); final analysis planned at 130 events.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **DASL very high-risk** pts getting radical RT (ISUP GG5, GG4 with cT2b-T4 / rT3a-T4 / PSA >20 ng/mL, or cN1) or **salvage RT** for PSA persistence or rise ≥0.1 ng/mL within 12 mo with pN1/cN1, GG5, or GG4 pT3a-pT4. Stratified by prior RP, planned docetaxel, pelvic N1.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Darolutamide 600 mg BID x 96 wk** vs placebo. Both arms got **96 wk ADT**. Docetaxel use was allowed as a stratification factor.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: **prostate/bed + pelvic LNs**. Dose, fractionation and imaging used for staging are not reported in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** MFS by conventional imaging (MFS-CI). **Secondary:** OS, PCSS, PSA-PFS, time to subsequent hormonal therapy, time to castration resistance, AEs, HRQoL.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary met at interim, **HR 0.42 (0.27-0.66), p=0.0001**, against a rejection boundary of 0.012. Authors report the benefit was consistent across all subgroups (no subgroup HRs in source).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Authors describe the treatment burden as **similar to placebo**. No AE rates or grade breakdown in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: This sits alongside ENZARAD and the STAMPEDE M0 abiraterone work, which ask the same ARPI-plus-RT intensification question. DASL-HiCaP is the placebo-controlled test, it mandates pelvic nodal RT in both arms, and it includes an early-salvage cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents DASL very high-risk pts getting radical or early salvage RT to the prostate/bed and pelvic nodes with 2y ADT. Does not represent pts treated without pelvic nodal RT, with shorter ADT, or with metastatic disease on conventional imaging.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Event-driven interim with **only 27 vs 63 events**, so the estimate may shrink by the final analysis. MFS is read on **conventional imaging**, which may not match PSMA-staged practice. **Primary vs salvage** results are not shown separately.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The drug's effect is **on metastases**, not competing mortality, which supports a real anticancer benefit. Whether it becomes an OS benefit at PCSS HR 0.58 and OS HR 0.88 is still unknown.

studies.interpretation:
DASL-HiCaP asks the question that STAMPEDE's M0 abiraterone comparison and ENZARAD have circled for years: in a non-metastatic, very high-risk population already getting RT and long-course ADT, does adding a next-generation androgen receptor inhibitor change the natural history? What sets it apart is the control arm. Both arms got prostate or prostate-bed RT with pelvic nodes and 96 weeks of ADT, so the comparator is close to the most intensive local and hormonal backbone in current use, not an under-treated control. Any benefit here is on top of that backbone, which matters for an RT reader who already treats this group with nodal fields.

The split of events is the most informative detail. Metastases accounted for 9 of 27 events with darolutamide and 46 of 63 with placebo, while deaths without prior metastases were 18 and 17. Competing mortality is flat and distant failure is cut sharply. That pattern is what a real anticancer effect looks like, and it argues against the worry that a composite surrogate is being moved by noise. It also means that in the darolutamide arm about two-thirds of MFS events are now non-metastatic deaths. That has two consequences. Further MFS gains will be hard to see, and the OS signal will be diluted by deaths the drug cannot prevent. The interim OS HR of 0.88 with a CI from 0.49 to 1.59 says nothing yet.

The interim design calls for some restraint. Stopping at 87 of 130 planned events with a p-value well inside its boundary is legitimate, but early-stopped trials tend to overstate effect sizes, and an HR of 0.42 based on 90 total events has a wide interval. The endpoint is read on conventional imaging. A PSMA-staged population would likely enroll fewer occult-metastatic pts, which could lower the control-arm event rate and shrink the absolute benefit, though the relative effect may hold. The source also does not separate the radical-RT and salvage cohorts. These are biologically different groups, and the claim of a consistent subgroup effect comes without numbers.

For practice, the strongest supported read is darolutamide added to 2 years of ADT and pelvic nodal RT in pts meeting these specific criteria. The authors report limited extra treatment burden, but no AE rates are in the source, so the toxicity trade-off can't yet be judged against the competing ARPI options. The trial does not address shorter ADT, prostate-only fields, or whether the drug can replace some of the ADT. The final analysis and mature OS will decide whether the authors' 'new paradigm' framing is borne out or turns out to be an early-stopping overestimate.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Darolutamide cut metastases (9 vs 46) even though both arms got pelvic nodal RT and 96 wk ADT, so nodal coverage did not remove the distant-failure risk the drug addresses. The result covers both radical and early salvage RT. Dose/fractionation is not in the source, so it can't be checked against your own regimen.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The secondary endpoints all point the same way: time to CRPC HR 0.22 (0.09-0.52) and subsequent hormonal therapy HR 0.36 (0.21-0.60). This makes darolutamide the ARPI with placebo-controlled data alongside 2y ADT and RT. OS HR 0.88 (0.49-1.59) is still immature.

open_questions: Does the MFS benefit translate to OS at final analysis?
Is benefit similar in salvage vs radical RT cohorts?
Does the effect hold in PSMA-PET staged pts?

🔍 HR LPC/LAPC, conventionally staged M0; no baseline PSMA PET

💊 APA 240 mg QD + ADT: C1-C6 neoadjuvant, RP + PLND, then C7-C12 adjuvant
🔍 Control: RP + PLND, then local or systemic adjuvant tx at physician discretion
📊 1° EP EFS (BCF, LRR, DM or death): HR 0.38 (95% CI 0.26-0.55), p<0.0001
📐 MFS (HR 0.49) and TTST (HR 0.29) carry nominal p-values only

details.text: ⚠️ Discussant critique (Nicholas van As)
subdetails: No PSMA PET at diagnosis; occult PSMA-avid disease possible at baseline
MFS events mostly PSMA PET-detected: true progression or delayed detection cannot be separated
~70% of RP pts with PSMA PET-detected relapse had persistent PSA

details: ⚠️ T recovery to ≥200 ng/dL: median 20.7 mo (~9 mo from EOT); PSA-driven EFS partly read under residual castration
🔗 proPSMA: staging accuracy 92% PSMA PET vs 65% CT + bone scan (discussant slide)
⚠️ AE magnitudes (all-grade hot flush) truncated in source tweet; no toxicity numbers available

verdict.audience: HR LPC/LAPC, conventionally staged M0, planned RP + PLND

studies.significance: The testosterone curve is the hidden read: T recovery to ≥200 ng/dL took a median 20.7 mo (~9 mo from EOT), so much of the EFS window is BCF assessed under residual castration. TTST medians of 46.0 vs 12.3 mo carry ~20 mo of lead-time, which leaves the durable-benefit question with MFS and its nominal p=0.0193.
studies.monday_clinic: In conventionally staged HR LPC/LAPC headed for RP + PLND, this supports perioperative APA + ADT as an EFS-delaying option under discussion; it does not extend to PSMA PET-staged pts or to men treated with definitive RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized 1:3, open-label**, N=408, accrual July 2022 to October 2023. Stratified by cN0 vs cN1, Gleason 7 vs 8-10, and region. Phase not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **HR LPC/LAPC, conventionally staged M0** (CT + bone scan). **No baseline PSMA PET.**

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **APA 240 mg QD + ADT** for 6 cycles neoadjuvant, RP + PLND, then 6 cycles adjuvant. Control: RP + PLND with **local or systemic adjuvant tx at physician discretion**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** EFS, time to first BCF (PSA progression), LRR, DM or death. **Secondary/exploratory:** MFS, time to first subsequent therapy.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **EFS HR 0.38** (0.26-0.55), p<0.0001; **MFS HR 0.49** (0.26-0.90), nominal p=0.0193; **TTST HR 0.29** (0.20-0.43), nominal. Per-arm values in the figure captions.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: proPSMA showed PSMA PET staging accuracy of 92% vs 65% for CT + bone scan, and EAU/ESMO advise PSMA PET/CT for high-risk disease where available. PROTEUS staged without it, so its M0 population differs from a modern PSMA-staged cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents conventionally staged M0 HR LPC/LAPC treated with RP + PLND. Does not represent PSMA PET-staged pts or men treated with definitive RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **1:3 allocation** leaves 102 pts in the experimental arm. The control adjuvant strategy was at physician discretion, so the comparator is heterogeneous. Safety magnitudes were truncated in the source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Lead-time from treatment exposure and slow testosterone recovery inflate the early-window endpoints. Whether metastatic progression is truly delayed, rather than PSMA-avid disease being detected later, **is not settled** without baseline PSMA PET.

studies.interpretation:
The headline EFS hazard ratio of 0.38 is large, but the endpoint's components decide how far it can carry. EFS here is the first of biochemical failure, locoregional recurrence, distant metastasis or death. In a post-prostatectomy population, biochemical failure will dominate that composite, and the trial's own testosterone data show why that matters: recovery to 200 ng/dL took a median of 20.7 months, roughly nine months after treatment ended. A meaningful part of the follow-up therefore measured PSA in men who were still functionally castrate. A PSA endpoint read under residual androgen suppression measures exposure to therapy as much as disease biology, and an EFS separation of this size is what one would expect from that mechanism alone, whether or not the underlying disease course changed.

The secondary endpoints were meant to answer that, and they only partly do. Time to first subsequent therapy (medians 46.0 vs 12.3 months) is vulnerable to the same problem, and the discussant estimated about 20 months of lead-time bias. MFS is the endpoint that could show durable benefit, and its hazard ratio of 0.49 has a wide interval (0.26-0.90) and a nominal p-value. The detection table also matters: most metastatic events were found on PSMA PET (9 vs 50 events), in a trial that staged its population with CT and bone scan alone. Van As's point is that an event called new metastasis may be disease that was present at baseline and only found later. Detection timing could differ between arms if hormonal therapy temporarily suppressed PSMA-avid disease, so the MFS difference may reflect when disease was found rather than whether it developed.

The population is also behind current staging. EAU and ESMO now advise PSMA PET for high-risk disease where available, and proPSMA's accuracy figures (92% vs 65%) suggest some enrolled men had occult nodal or distant disease. In a PSMA-staged population the absolute benefit could plausibly be smaller, because the men most likely to have early events would be identified and treated differently from the start.

Two design features limit the comparison further. The 1:3 allocation leaves 102 men in the experimental arm, which makes the secondary endpoints fragile. The control arm received adjuvant local or systemic treatment at the physician's discretion, so the comparator is not one defined strategy, and the source does not say how much adjuvant or salvage RT the control arm received.

What would change the read is maturation of MFS to a non-nominal result, ideally with OS, and some evidence that the effect holds once testosterone has fully recovered. Until then, this trial shows that perioperative apalutamide plus ADT delays PSA-defined events after prostatectomy. It does not yet show that it changes the metastatic course of the disease.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: Testosterone recovery took a median 20.7 mo (~9 mo from EOT), so the EFS gain is partly measured during residual castration. MFS HR 0.49 with nominal p=0.0193 is the endpoint that will decide whether perioperative APA + ADT changes disease course or only delays PSA events.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: The surgical backbone was unchanged (RP + PLND in both arms), and the control arm's adjuvant management was left to physician discretion. Without baseline PSMA PET, some conventionally staged M0 candidates may have had occult disease, which matters when selecting HR LPC/LAPC pts for RP.

open_questions: Does the EFS benefit hold in PSMA PET-staged M0 pts?
Will MFS reach non-nominal significance with longer follow-up?
Does any benefit persist after testosterone recovery?

studies.name: Low-Dose Involved Field RT in Indolent Lymphomas
studies.tldr: 4 Gy involved-field RT in recurrent indolent lymphoma: ORR 92%, CR 61%, median time to local progression 25 mo, toxicity virtually absent.
details: 🔍 Phase II, N=109 assessable (111 treated), 304 symptomatic sites, Nov 1997 to Mar 2002
🔍 Recurrent symptomatic B-cell indolent lymphoma: FL 98 (43 G1, 55 G2), MALT 9, lymphoplasmacytoid 2
🔍 Heavily pretreated: median 2 prior regimens (range 0-11); median 41 mo since diagnosis
🔍 Bulky disease (≥5 cm) in 48 of 92 pts with size data (52%); 13% had nodes ≥10 cm
📐 RT: 4 Gy as 2×2 Gy 48h apart (n=80) or 1×4 Gy (n=29); whole nodal area or node + 1.5 cm margin
📊 in-field control: CR 61%, PR 31%, SD 6%, PD 2%; median TP 14 mo, median TLP 25 mo

details.text: 📊 Median time to progression by response to first LD-IF-RT

details: 📊 Re-treatment in 41 selected responders: RR 98%, CR 71%, PR 27%
📊 Response not associated with age, FL grade, RT schedule, prior lines, site count, or node size
📊 Toxicity: 1 transient alopecia, 1 transient hyperpigmentation; no tumor lysis
🔗 RR slightly better than pts' own 2nd (P=.04) and last (P=.03) prior regimens
🔗 vs Girinsky (Paris, 48 pts): concordant RR/CR, but 2yr local PFS in PR pts 46% there vs 10% here
⚠️ Median follow-up for pts in remission only 7 mo; durability estimates fragile
⚠️ Within-pt comparison vs prior regimens is historical, confounded by line and disease biology
⚠️ CR signals for ≤2 sites (P=.01) and ≤5 cm (P=.006) are multiple-comparison, not definitive
⚠️ 10 pts transformed to DLBCL; median TP only 3 mo despite similar response rates

verdict.rationale: Single-cohort phase II, no randomized comparator vs conventional-dose RT or systemic therapy; within-patient historical comparison, 7-mo median follow-up in remitters.
verdict.audience: Recurrent symptomatic indolent B-cell lymphoma (mostly FL G1-2), pretreated

studies.significance: The dose is the read: 2×2 Gy produced CR 61% with near-zero toxicity, and the 41 selected responders re-treated reached RR 98%, so the field can be re-irradiated. CR pts held local control for a median 42 mo, while PR pts progressed in-field at 10 mo, which frames 4 Gy as palliation that is durable mainly when it achieves CR.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pretreated pt with recurrent symptomatic FL grade 1-2, this supports 4 Gy involved-field RT as a low-toxicity palliative option, repeatable on response; it does not address transformed disease or curative-intent early-stage FL.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase II** protocol, single cohort, **N=109** assessable of 111 treated, 304 irradiated sites. Response assessed 4-6 wk post-RT then every 3 mo; median follow-up for pts in remission **7 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Symptomatic recurrent B-cell indolent lymphoma**; proven transformation and concurrent steroids or chemo excluded. Median age 62, median **2 prior regimens** (range 0-11), bulky disease in 52% of pts with size data.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **4 Gy** as **2×2 Gy** 48h apart (n=80) or **1×4 Gy** (n=29), megavoltage photons or electrons. Target was the entire nodal area or the node with a **1.5 cm margin**, involved sites only; 6 pts had total nodal irradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **in-field lymphoma control**, response defined by local activity only, worst site counted. Secondary: TP (any progression) and TLP (in-field), Kaplan-Meier from first RT day.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **ORR 92%**, CR 61%, PR 31%. Median **TP 14 mo**, **TLP 25 mo**; CR pts TLP **42 mo**. Re-treatment in 41 selected responders: **RR 98%**, CR 71%.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity **virtually absent**: one transient alopecia, one transient hyperpigmentation. Antiemetics for upper abdominal fields; allopurinol for bulky disease, no gout or tumor lysis.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Concordant with **Girinsky et al** (135 sites, 48 pts) on RR, CR and inferior bulky-site results, but **2yr local PFS in PR pts 46% there vs 10% here**. FORT later tested this low-dose approach against conventional-dose RT in a randomized design.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pretreated pts with recurrent symptomatic FL grade 1-2 and other indolent B-cell histologies. Does not represent transformed disease, FL grade 3, or untreated early-stage FL.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Comparison with pts' **own prior regimens** is historical and confounded by line of therapy, with power falling as numbers drop. Prognostic CR signals (**≤2 sites P=.01, ≤5 cm P=.006**) sit amid many tests; mixed target-volume definitions left to physician discretion.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A **local, repeatable, near-toxicity-free** option for systemic disease, with response rates matching first-line systemic therapy in this cohort. It does not settle whether 4 Gy matches conventional dose for durability, particularly in PR or bulky sites.

studies.interpretation:
The core claim here is that 4 Gy, a dose low enough to be almost free of toxicity, induces response in nearly every pt with recurrent indolent lymphoma, and that response can be repeated. The response rate itself is the least surprising part. Indolent B-cell lymphoma is exquisitely radiosensitive, and the Paris series from Girinsky's group had already reported similar response and CR rates on a site-based analysis. What this cohort adds is scale, a patient-based analysis, and the attempt to anchor the result against the same pts' earlier regimens.

That anchoring deserves the most skepticism. Comparing LD-IF-RT with each pt's prior chemotherapy line is a within-pt historical comparison, and the direction of bias is not obvious. Later lines in FL typically perform worse, which flatters a regimen given late, yet LD-IF-RT here was also given to symptomatic, often bulky, frequently refractory disease, which handicaps it. The reported edge over the second (P=.04) and last (P=.03) regimens is modest, sits among several comparisons, and loses power as the denominator shrinks with each line. The defensible reading is not superiority but rough parity with systemic therapy in a time-without-treatment sense, at a fraction of the toxicity.

The pattern of failure is the more clinically useful signal. CR pts held in-field control for a median 42 mo, whereas PR pts progressed in-field almost immediately (TLP 10 mo, essentially equal to TP). Response depth, not just response, predicts durability. The discrepancy with Girinsky on exactly this point, 2-year local progression-free rates in PR pts of 46% versus 10%, may reflect the Paris cohort's inclusion of stage I-II disease, as the authors suggest, or chance. Either way it should temper any expectation that a partial response to 4 Gy buys lasting local control. The hints that CR is less likely in pts with more than two sites or nodes over 5 cm fit radiobiological intuition, but the authors correctly decline to treat them as established given the number of tests.

Follow-up is the binding constraint on everything above. A median follow-up of 7 mo among pts still in remission means the 42-mo TLP for CR pts and the multi-year progression-free estimates rest on few pts at risk. Ten transformations, with a median TP of 3 mo despite ordinary initial response, are a reminder that rapid regression at 4 Gy does not distinguish indolent from transforming biology; a pt whose site fails quickly after low-dose RT warrants rebiopsy rather than a second course.

For practice, the study legitimized very low-dose RT as palliation in relapsed indolent lymphoma and established that re-irradiation is feasible, which matters for a disease with a decades-long relapsing course. It does not tell the reader whether 4 Gy is as durable as conventional palliative or definitive doses; that question required a randomized comparison, which FORT later undertook. It also predates routine rituximab use, so its parity claim against systemic therapy was made against older chemotherapy backbones and cannot be transferred directly to modern systemic options. What would make the result misleading is if durable control proved confined to small, non-bulky CR sites, leaving the headline response rate to overstate benefit for the bulky symptomatic disease that most often prompts referral.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 2×2 Gy produced CR 61% with near-zero toxicity, and re-treatment of selected responders gave RR 98%, so the field can be re-irradiated. In-field control was durable in CR pts (median TLP 42 mo) but not PR pts (10 mo), and the bulky and multi-site CR signals point to where 4 Gy may fall short.

open_questions: Does 4 Gy match conventional-dose RT for durable local control?
Optimal role of low-dose RT alongside modern anti-CD20 therapy

studies.name: Nonspine Bone Metastases SBRT Practice Patterns
studies.tldr: 35 Gy/5 most often chosen (29/99 responses); 40 Gy/5 acceptable to 8 or 9 of 9 experts wherever listed; every schedule BED ≤100 Gy10.

details.text: 🔍 Survey of 9 international NSBM-SBRT experts on 11 nonsurgical cases, GTV pre-contoured; descriptive analysis only
🔍 Case sites covered
subdetails: Pelvis: ilium, ischium, acetabulum, pubic symphysis

details.text: 📊 Schedules chosen by ≥3 experts (single dose volume)

rows: Most common: 29 of 99 responses (29%); 5 experts in ≥1 case

details.text: 📊 BED range 48 to 100 Gy10; 58% of schedules at BED 60 Gy10
📊 SIB used routinely by 3 of 9; 30 Gy/3 + 15-24 Gy/3 most common SIB (12 of 24, 50%)
📊 40 Gy/5 most widely accepted: unanimous (n=9) or near-unanimous (n=8) in every case listed
⚠️ Schedules a majority rated not recommended, by case
📊 Dose de-escalation triggers (experts of 9)

Prior cRT to same target >3 mo ago: 7

details: 📊 Escalation a minority choice: radioresistant histology (n=3), bulky tumor (n=1), extraosseous disease (n=1)
📊 Unanimous no change for mild cortical erosion or non-weight-bearing bone with moderate-severe erosion

details.text: 📊 MRI fusion routine for 5 experts (56%); 2 CT-only, 2 fuse selectively
🔗 vs Erler et al (cited): LC 95% at 6 mo, 87% at 24 mo, 106 NSBM after 30-35 Gy/5

details: ⚠️ No formal consensus process; acceptability ratings are opinion, not LC or fracture outcomes

details.text: ⚠️ BED calculated at α/β 10; authors note lower α/β may apply to breast and prostate cases

verdict.rationale: Expert practice survey (n=9) with acceptability ratings; no formal consensus process and no clinical outcomes, so it maps opinion rather than testing efficacy.
verdict.audience: Nonsurgical nonspine bone metastases considered for SBRT

studies.significance: The site-specific rejections are the RT read: 20 Gy/1 lost majority support in the humerus, acetabulum and femur cases, and 50 Gy/5 in the humerus and acetabulum, while 40 Gy/5 stayed acceptable to 8 or 9 of 9 wherever listed. For weight-bearing or periarticular targets, that favors moderate 5-fraction schedules over single fraction.
studies.monday_clinic: For a nonsurgical nonspine bone met irradiated >3 months ago, this survey supports dose de-escalation (all 9 experts after prior SBRT, 7 of 9 after prior cRT); it does not address spine targets or postoperative bone.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Two-round survey of **9 international radiation oncologists** chosen for NSBM-SBRT expertise, covering **11 cases** with planning CT, MRI and GTV contours supplied. Round 2 rated each proposed schedule acceptable / not recommended / no opinion and picked 2 preferred schedules; majority defined as **≥5 of 9**. Completion was 100%.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Nonsurgical nonspine bone metastases** across long bones, pelvis and thorax, with RCC, breast, NSCLC and prostate primaries; some cases carried an extraosseous component.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: 6 experts prescribed **one dose volume**, 3 used an **SIB** with GTV/CTV or nested CTV1/CTV2 volumes. Schedules spanned 18-24 Gy/1 to 42-50 Gy/10, all at **BED ≤100 Gy10**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **35 Gy/5** was chosen most (29 of 99 responses), and **40 Gy/5** was the most widely accepted. Scapula was the only case where every schedule had majority acceptance. Humerus, acetabulum and femur were the only cases where a majority rejected one or more schedules.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The ≤100 Gy10 ceiling sits below the **BED >100 Gy10** recommended for lung and liver SBRT. The cited Erler series reported **LC 95% and 87% at 6 and 24 mo** after 30-35 Gy/5, with **8.5% fracture** at a median 2.5 mo; a second series of 85 NSBM reported **1-yr LC 92%**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents nonsurgical nonspine bone metastases treated with SBRT by experienced centers. Does not represent spine SBRT, postoperative bone, or settings where OAR constraints force de-escalation.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: BED equivalence assumes **α/β 10** across histologies, which the authors concede may not hold for breast and prostate. Health-system and resource differences across the panel may drive part of the variation attributed to judgment.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The heterogeneity is real but bounded: a moderate-BED, 5-fraction working range emerges, and caution concentrates on **weight-bearing long bones and joints**. The optimal dose balancing LC and fracture stays unknown, and the authors call for phase I dose-finding and comparative trials.

studies.interpretation:
The useful output of this survey is not the heterogeneity it headlines but the boundaries around it. Nine experienced NSBM-SBRT practitioners prescribed dozens of different schedules, yet none exceeded BED 100 Gy10, five-fraction regimens dominated, and 40 Gy/5 drew acceptance from all or all but one expert in every case where it appeared. Read that way, the paper describes a de facto working range for nonspine bone SBRT at a time when prospective dose data for these sites are close to absent.

The ceiling is the most interesting finding. Lung and liver SBRT practice anchors on BED above 100 Gy10, and this panel deliberately stayed under it. The authors attribute the restraint to fracture caution, and the site-level rejections support that reading: single-fraction 20 Gy/1 lost majority support in the humerus, acetabulum and femur cases, and 50 Gy/5 in the humerus and acetabulum. The panel is effectively treating weight-bearing long bones and periarticular targets as their own toxicity class. Whether that caution is warranted cannot be settled from the fracture data available. The cited series reported 8.5% fracture after 30-35 Gy/5, but most of those events were in ribs and iliac bones, not the long bones that worried the panel.

Whether the lower dose costs local control is the open question. The retrospective data the authors cite, LC 95% and 87% at 6 and 24 months in the Erler series and 1-year LC 92% in a second series of 85 lesions, suggest the moderate range performs acceptably. Both are retrospective, histologically mixed, and short relative to the survival horizon of an oligometastatic pt. If control erodes beyond two years in radioresistant histologies, the minority who escalated for radioresistant disease may turn out to be right, and a uniform ceiling would be the wrong lesson.

Confidence should be calibrated to the method. This is nine selected experts rating contoured scenarios, with no Delphi iteration, no outcomes, and a panel spread across health systems with different resources. The α/β 10 convention is a simplification the authors acknowledge for the breast and prostate cases, so schedules that share BED 60 Gy10 are only approximately equivalent across histologies. The unanimous de-escalation after prior SBRT is a reasonable instinct, but the authors themselves note the risk profile of salvage NSBM-SBRT is not well characterized.

What it changes: for a nonsurgical nonspine target, 35 Gy/5 and 40 Gy/5 are defensible defaults with broad expert backing, and single fraction in a weight-bearing long bone or acetabulum now carries a documented majority objection. What it does not do is define an optimal dose or show that the site-specific caution prevents fractures. Those require the dose-finding and comparative trials the authors call for.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Site drives the objections: a majority rejected 20 Gy/1 in the humerus, acetabulum and femur cases and 50 Gy/5 in the humerus and acetabulum, while 40 Gy/5 kept 8 or 9 of 9 votes everywhere listed. For weight-bearing or periarticular NSBM, moderate 5-fraction schedules have the broadest expert backing.

studies.tldr: 3-mo ITT pain response 38% vs 21% (P=.05) with 12-16 Gy single-fraction SBRT vs 30 Gy/10; 2-yr local PFS 100% vs 75.6%.
details: 🔍 Phase 2, nonblinded, randomized noninferiority trial, single institution (MD Anderson), N=160
🔍 Noninferiority margin 10%, one-sided alpha 0.20, 90% power
🔍 SBRT 12 or 16 Gy x1 by lesion size (4 cm cutoff) vs 30 Gy in 10 fx
🔍 PTV = GTV + 5 mm, no CTV; stereotactic immobilization in SBRT arm

details.text: 📊 Pain response (CR+PR) by timepoint, SBRT vs MFRT
📊 Pain response by dose (SBRT ITT subset vs MFRT)
📊 Local control and retreatment
📐 HRs at 3 mo, SBRT vs MFRT (ITT)

details: 📊 Median OS 6.7 mo in both arms; no OS difference

details.text: 📊 Toxicity: no between-arm differences reported

details: ⚠️ Superiority claims rest on per-protocol analyses: 44 of 81 vs 35 of 79 analyzed at 3 mo
⚠️ Prophylactic dexamethasone recommended for SBRT arm only, biasing early pain response
⚠️ Comparator is 30 Gy/10, not 8 Gy single fraction
⚠️ 16 Gy assigned to smaller lesions, so dose effect is confounded by lesion size

verdict.rationale: Single-institution randomized phase 2 with one-sided alpha 0.20; superiority signals are per-protocol amid heavy attrition, comparator 30 Gy/10 rather than 8 Gy. Authors call for phase 3.
verdict.audience: Painful, predominantly nonspine bone mets, life expectancy >3 mo, no prior RT

studies.significance: Dose, not single fraction per se, carries the pain signal: 3-mo ITT response was 62% (13 of 21) with 16 Gy vs 30% (18 of 60) with 12 Gy, and 12 Gy tracked 30 Gy/10 at 9 mo (13.3% vs 15.2%). Because 16 Gy went to smaller lesions, the dose choice remains hypothesis-level.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a painful nonspine bone met, good performance status and longer expected survival, this supports single-fraction SBRT as a reasonable alternative to 30 Gy/10; it does not test SBRT against an 8 Gy single fraction or extend to spine lesions, cord compression or pathologic fracture.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 2, nonblinded, randomized noninferiority** trial at one institution, 1:1, **N=160** (81 SBRT, 79 MFRT). Stratified by tumor size, bone site and number of sites irradiated. Enrolled September 2014 to June 2018.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pathologic cancer diagnosis, **painful bone mets (score ≥2 of 10)**, age ≥18, **life expectancy >3 mo**; up to 3 fields allowed. Excluded prior RT to the site, untreated cord compression, pathologic fracture at the site, and recent radioisotope.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 12 or 16 Gy x1** by lesion size (4 cm cutoff) vs **30 Gy in 10 fx**. PTV = GTV + 5 mm, no CTV; 2D/3D, IMRT or VMAT delivery. Prophylactic 7-day low-dose dexamethasone recommended for SBRT only.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** pain response by international consensus criteria (pain score plus MED), noninferiority margin 10%. **Secondary:** MDASI QoL, CTCAE toxicity, local control, OS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No toxicity differences** between arms. G3 fatigue 9.9% vs 5.1% (P=.37), fracture 1.2% vs 0% (P=.99); MDASI scores improved in both arms without a difference.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Prior randomized trials found no pain difference between single and multifraction conventional courses, with more retreatment after 8 Gy. RTOG 9714 and the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study are the conventional-dose trials behind that equivalence. This trial escalates the single fraction but never tests it against 8 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with painful, predominantly nonspine bone mets, good expected survival and no prior RT to the site. Does not represent spine lesions, cord compression, pathologic fracture, or the 8 Gy single-fraction decision.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Dexamethasone given asymmetrically** to SBRT pts confounds early pain response. The **16 vs 12 Gy contrast is non-randomized** and tracks lesion size. Five SBRT pts did not receive treatment due to insurance denial, and median OS of 6.7 mo leaves few pts at risk for late local failure.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The ITT data support **noninferiority** and a local-control advantage for SBRT; the superiority read depends on per-protocol denominators. The live question is **16 Gy vs 8 Gy** in pts selected for longer survival, which needs a phase 3.

studies.interpretation:
The trial answers a narrower question than its headline suggests. The comparator is 30 Gy in 10 fractions, a regimen that prior randomized work had already shown to be no better for pain than a short single-fraction course, which mostly costs more retreatment. RTOG 9714 and the Dutch Bone Metastasis Study are the conventional-dose trials behind that equivalence. So this result is best read as escalated single-fraction SBRT against a protracted conventional course, not against the single-fraction standard most departments default to. Whether 16 Gy beats 8 Gy, the decision that actually sits in front of a palliative clinic, is untested here.

Within that frame the signal runs in one direction. The ITT pain response difference at 3 months (38% vs 21%, P=.05), the local-control separation (2-yr local PFS 100% vs 75.6%) and the narcotic-escalation HR of 0.26 all favour SBRT. But the trial was powered for noninferiority with a one-sided alpha of 0.20, a permissive phase 2 threshold, and the superiority language rests mostly on per-protocol comparisons that analyzed 44 of 81 and 35 of 79 pts at 3 months. Pts who die early or deteriorate leave per-protocol denominators, and if that attrition differs by arm in ways linked to pain, the gap can widen without any treatment effect. The ITT figures are the ones to carry into a tumor board.

Two design features push the pain endpoint toward SBRT independent of dose. Prophylactic dexamethasone was recommended for the SBRT arm only, and steroids blunt early pain and flare; the 2-week per-protocol separation is exactly where that would show. The dose subset is also confounded, since 16 Gy went to the smaller lesions, so the 16 vs 12 Gy contrast mixes dose with tumour size. The finding that 12 Gy pain response at 9 months sat close to 30 Gy/10 (13.3% vs 15.2%) is the cautionary half of that subset and deserves as much weight as the 16 Gy result.

Local control is the cleaner secondary. Zero local failures with SBRT against a rising cumulative incidence with MFRT is coherent with the BED gap, but events were few (HR 0.18, 95% CI 0.02-1.47) and median OS was 6.7 months in both arms, so most pts did not live long enough for local failure to matter. That tension defines who the result applies to: a durable local benefit is plausible in the minority with long expected survival, and those pts were a small share of this cohort despite the life-expectancy entry criterion.

For an RT reader, the trial supports SBRT as a reasonable option for selected nonspine lesions in pts with good performance status and longer expected survival, and it argues that the confirmatory phase 3 should be run against 8 Gy rather than 30 Gy/10. It does not establish superiority for pain, and its single-institution design with size-assigned dosing makes the preference for 16 Gy a hypothesis rather than a finding.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Dose carries the pain signal: 3-mo ITT response was 62% (13 of 21) with 16 Gy vs 30% (18 of 60) with 12 Gy, and 12 Gy tracked 30 Gy/10 at 9 mo. Local failure was 0% with SBRT at 24 mo, but 16 Gy went to smaller lesions, so the dose pick is hypothesis-level.

Single-Fraction Stereotactic vs Conventional Multifraction Radiotherapy for Pain Relief in Patients With Predominantly Nonspine Bone Metastases
High Response Rates and Lasting Remissions After Low-Dose Involved Field Radiotherapy in Indolent Lymphomas
papers.abstract: Purpose: To study the response rates and duration of response after low-dose (4 Gy) involved field radiotherapy (LD-IF-RT) in patients with recurrent indolent lymphoma. Patients and Methods: A total of 109 assessable patients (304 symptomatic sites) were irradiated (53 males and 56 females; median age, 62 years; range, 35 to 93), including 98 patients with follicular lymphoma (43 grade 1 and 55 grade 2), nine extranodal marginal zone lymphomas of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue-type and two patients with lymphoplasmacytoid lymphoma. Bulky disease (≥5 cm) was present in 52% of all patients. A median of two prior regimens (range, 0 to 11) preceded LD-IF-RT. The median time since diagnosis was 41 months (range, 2 to 358 months). Time to (local) progression was calculated according to the Kaplan-Meier method. Differences in response rates between treatments within the same patient were compared using the McNemar test. Results: The overall response rate was 92%; complete response was reached in 67 patients (61%), partial response in 34 patients (31%), stable disease in six patients (6%), and progressive disease in two patients (2%). The median time to progression was 14 months. The median time to local progression was 25 months. The 67 patients with complete response showed a median time to progression of 25 months and a median time to local progression of 42 months. None of the factors studied (age, sex, follicular lymphoma grade, radiotherapy regimen, number of previous regimens and previous history, number of positive sites or largest lymphoma diameter) were found to be related to response rate. Conclusion: LD-IF-RT is a valuable asset in the management of patients with follicular lymphoma and should be considered in patients with recurrent disease.
